name: Deleting Divisors
description: Alice and Bob are playing a game. They start with a positive integer $$$n$$$ and take alternating turns doing operations on it. Each turn a player can subtract from $$$n$$$ one of its divisors that isn't $$$1$$$ or $$$n$$$. The player who cannot make a move on his/her turn loses. Alice always moves first. Note that they subtract a divisor of the current number in each turn. You are asked to find out who will win the game if both players play optimally.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Then $$$t$$$ test cases follow. Each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^9$$$) — the initial number.
output_specification: For each test case output " Alice " if Alice will win the game or " Bob " if Bob will win, if both players play optimally.
subsubtopic: 472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory
approach_summary: Compute Sprague-Grundy values g(u) = mex({g(v) : u -> v}). Game state is winning iff XOR sum of independent game components is non-zero.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1537D — Deleting Divisors [472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory]
topic_editorial.summary: Impartial game theory via Sprague-Grundy theorem.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Any finite, impartial game under normal play convention is equivalent to a one-pile game of Nim with pile size equal to its Grundy value $g(u) = \text{mex}(\{g(v) : u \to v\})$. A compound game of independent subgames is winning for the first player if and only if $\bigoplus_{i} g_i \ne 0$.
